title: The leper by the fire
hookLine: a man with leprosy scratches his sores by the fire and calls it pleasure

cards: A mosquito bite on the ankle. Scratching it is a bad idea, it gets scratched anyway, and for a few seconds that feels like relief. Then it's worse.
A wandering ascetic named Māgandiya hears that the Buddha teaches restraint of the senses, and he's offended. He calls the Buddha a destroyer of growth, someone who kills off life's pleasures.
The Buddha doesn't get defensive. He tells Māgandiya about his own youth: three palaces, one for each season, musicians, pleasures on offer. He gave it all up.
Why would anyone do that? He answers with a picture far stronger than a mosquito bite.

teach.h: SORES, AND A PIT OF COALS.
teach.b: Suppose, the Buddha says, there were a man with leprosy, his body covered in sores. His only relief is to scratch the sores with his nails and hold his body over a pit of burning coals. The heat eases the itch.
Now suppose a physician comes and cures him. He's healthy, free, able to go where he likes.

teach.h: THE FIRE IS THE SAME. HE ISN'T.
teach.b: Would he envy another sick man scratching by the fire? No. And if two strong men tried to drag him toward the coals, he'd twist and fight to get away.
The coals are as hot as ever. What changed is his health. When he was sick, his senses were damaged, and so he took something painful to be pleasant.
That's the Buddha's point about cravings, and it isn't puritan. He doesn't say pleasure is evil. He says some of what we call pleasure is relief from an itch the craving itself keeps making.
The more you scratch, the more it itches.
Then the Buddha speaks a verse: health is the greatest gain, nibbāna the highest happiness. Māgandiya says he has heard those very words from his own teachers. So what is this health?
Māgandiya rubs his own arms and legs: this is health. The Buddha says he knows the words, but not yet what they point to.
A similar verse appears in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvâna the highest happiness."
The healed man doesn't hate the fire. He just doesn't need it anymore.

how: Buddhist teachers use this simile to explain why monastics and serious lay practitioners restrain the senses: not because pleasure is evil, but because craving feeds itself, and a calm mind finds deeper ease.

o: a pleasure the senses must give up
the brief relief of scratching an itch

games.q: the fire and the cure: tap the pairs.
p: called the Buddha a destroyer of growth
fights to keep away from the fire
the greatest gift, in the Dhammapada

s: the Buddha tells Māgandiya that all pleasure is evil
he says some 'pleasure' is relief from an itch that craving keeps making.
the Buddha describes his own youth in palaces
he tells Māgandiya he lived among pleasures, and gave them up.
once healed, the man would still enjoy the coals
the fire is unchanged, but he'd twist and fight to stay away from it.

games.q: you've been cured of a terrible itch. two strong men try to drag you back to the burning coals that once relieved it. what do you do?
o: twist and fight to get away
go, but only for a minute
games.why: the healed man resists with everything he has. what felt pleasant only felt that way because he was sick.

practice: Think of one thing you reach for that brings relief more than joy, checking, snacking, refreshing, rereading an old argument, and picture the moment just before you reach.
Feel the itch there, the restlessness, and breathe into it without scratching. Notice that it rises and, if you wait, begins to fade.

wordCard.voice: Sukha. A sick man finds relief in burning coals and calls it pleasure; once healed, he wouldn't go near them.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit sukha: ease, happiness, pleasure. the sutta asks what real sukha is.

carryVoice: Your line: the leper's fire. Relief from an itch isn't the same as ease. See you tomorrow.
